content: Dandruff, also known as scurf and historically referred to as Pityriasis capitis, is caused by the excessive shedding of dead skin cells from the scalp. While it is normal for skin cells to die and flake off, a small amount of flaking is common and not concerning. However, some individuals experience an abnormally high amount of flaking, either chronically or due to specific triggers. This excessive flaking may be accompanied by redness and irritation of the scalp. Dandruff is not caused by an organism like lice; it is simply an accumulation of dead skin cells on the scalp. It is also unlikely to be a direct cause of hair loss. In some cases, excessive flaking may be a symptom of other conditions such as seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, fungal infections, or excoriation due to head lice infestation. Dandruff is a widespread condition that can lead to social or self-esteem issues for many individuals. Treatment may be pursued for psychological reasons, even if the condition itself is not medically serious. The epidermal layer of the skin continuously renews itself, pushing older cells outward where they eventually die and flake off. In most people, these flakes are too small to be visible. However, in individuals with dandruff, the turnover of skin cells is unusually rapid, particularly on the scalp. Instead of the typical one-month cycle, skin cells in people with dandruff may mature and shed within 2 to 7 days. This accelerated process results in the shedding of large, oily clumps of dead skin cells, which appear as white or grayish patches on the scalp and clothing. Research has identified three key factors contributing to dandruff: 1. Sebum, or skin oil, produced by sebaceous glands. 2. Metabolic by-products of skin microorganisms, particularly Malassezia yeasts. 3. Individual susceptibility to these factors. Older literature often cited the fungus Malassezia furfur (formerly known as Pityrosporum ovale) as the cause of dandruff. However, more recent studies have identified Malassezia globosa, a scalp-specific fungus, as the primary agent. This fungus metabolizes triglycerides in sebum through the action of lipase, producing a lipid by-product called oleic acid (OA). In susceptible individuals, OA penetrates the stratum corneum (the outermost layer of the epidermis), triggering an inflammatory response. This disrupts the skin's homeostasis and leads to irregular shedding of stratum corneum cells. In rare cases, dandruff may result from an allergic reaction to chemicals in hair products such as gels, sprays, or oils, or even to certain dandruff treatments like ketoconazole. There is no strong evidence to suggest that diet (e.g., sugar or yeast), excessive sweating, or climate play a significant role in the development of dandruff. Seborrheic dermatitis, a condition characterized by flaking, redness, and itching, is closely related to dandruff. It often affects areas beyond the scalp, such as the folds around the nose and the eyebrows. Dry, thick, well-defined lesions with silvery scales may indicate scalp psoriasis, a less common condition. Factors such as seasonal changes, stress, and immunosuppression can exacerbate seborrheic dermatitis. Treatment for dandruff involves various strategies. Increasing the frequency of shampooing can help remove flakes, but eliminating the causative fungus leads to more significant improvement. Regular use of anti-fungal shampoos can reduce recurrence. Among anti-dandruff shampoos, those containing ketoconazole have been shown to be more effective than those with zinc pyrithione. Multiple studies have concluded that ketoconazole is the most effective anti-fungal agent for treating dandruff.
